report:
Conclusion: the claim is **supported for prescription, pharmaceutical-grade cannabidiol (CBD) as add-on therapy** in children/adolescents with Dravet syndrome, but it is not a cure and benefits come with adverse-effect and interaction risks.

In the pivotal randomized trial (120 patients, ages 2–18), median convulsive seizure frequency fell from 12.4 to 5.9 seizures/month with CBD versus 14.9 to 14.1 with placebo; ≥50% reduction occurred in 43% vs 27%, with more adverse events in the CBD group. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618?query=featured_home

A later dose-ranging RCT (n=199) found adjunctive CBD 10 and 20 mg/kg/day reduced convulsive seizures by 48.7% and 45.7% versus 26.9% for placebo, with better tolerability at 10 mg/kg/day. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7052786/

Regulators reflect this evidence: FDA labeling indicates Epidiolex for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome in patients ≥1 year. https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/210365s023lbl.pdf

However, NICE concluded CBD with clobazam reduces seizure frequency versus usual care while noting long-term efficacy after 3 years remains uncertain. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/TA614

Bottom line: evidence is strong for short-term reduction in convulsive seizures, moderate for sustained benefit; use should be specialist-supervised, with monitoring for somnolence, diarrhea, liver-enzyme elevations, and clobazam interactions.
